newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Saddam departure would end crisis in Gulf-Kuwait.
newsitem.headline: Saddam departure would end crisis in Gulf-Kuwait.

text.p: Kuwait on Saturday slammed as unacceptable Iraq's pledge to respect Western-imposed no-fly zones, saying the Gulf would remain unstable with Saddam Hussein in power in Baghdad.

The small state at the head of the Gulf stressed it was not advocating Saddam's overthrow but would discuss possible "future measures" against Iraq with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry when he visits Kuwait on Sunday.
"The crisis will never be over until Saddam Hussein goes. This cat and mouse game has to stop," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah told a news conference.
"We would like to see, once and for all, an end to this regime sooner rather than later...Some kind of measures will have to be taken to put an end to this," he added.
Kuwait has made similar statements during the periodic security flare-ups it has had with Iraq since the 1991 Gulf War ended a seven-month Iraqi occupation of the Gulf Arab state.

In the first official Kuwaiti reaction to Baghdad's promise not to attack Western aircraft patrolling the air exclusion zones, Sheikh Saud said: "This is an unacceptable way now...There is a clear violation here.
"He found a line of retreat and retreated. Saddam Hussein is now trying to retreat from his position concerning the no-fly zones," he added.

U.S.-led Western air forces in Turkey and the Gulf bar Iraqi flights north of the 36th parallel and south of the 33rd. Iraq said on Friday it had decided to suspend attacks on allied aircraft patrolling the zones until further notice.
With most regional allies unwilling to take part in the current U.S. military buildup, Washington is dispatching added warships to the region and 5,000 troops to Kuwait.
Eight Stealth radar-evading bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday as part of preparations for a possible military strike against Iraq.
Sheikh Saud, who was ambassador to Washington during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, said Kuwait "will never be caught unprepared again. We will take all necessary measures."

He said any military action against Iraq would not split the Gulf War multinational coalition, adding that media reports of disagreements between major powers and even among Kuwait's Gulf Arab allies over Iraq had been exaggerated.
"We are not just discussing side issues like no-fly zones. There are major issues we are talking about here, mainly the full implementation of U.N. Security Council resolution 687."

The April 1991 resolution established the ceasefire, guaranteed the inviolability of the Iraq-Kuwait border, set up U.N. observer forces on the border, launched the dismantling of Iraqi arms of mass destruction, set terms for war damage compensation and provided a framework for an eventual easing of sanctions imposed against Iraq since 1990.
